manifest.title: An array<array-key, int> argument cannot satisfy a parameter declared array<string, int>

ground_truth.statement: An array key is an int or a string and nothing else, and array-key is int|string, so an array declared array<array-key, int> is an array<int|string, int> and may contain int keys - the argument here contains the int key 0. The callee declares array<string, int> and applies strtoupper() to every key, which under strict_types fails with a TypeError on that int key. Passing an argument of type array<array-key, int> into a parameter of type array<string, int> is therefore unsound: the declared key type is a contract the argument cannot meet, and a diagnostic belongs on the call. PHP also normalises a numeric string key to int, so the caller cannot satisfy a string key type by spelling key 0 as '0' either.

phpstan.reason: PHPStan explicitly defines array-key as a permissive benevolent union rather than a strictly checked int|string alias. ArrayType normalizes that key to implicit mixed, and this baseline level-9 configuration leaves checkImplicitMixed disabled. Silence is therefore an excluded documented configuration-scope difference. An independent check with checkImplicitMixed: true emits argument.type on the unchanged fixture; the rule is implemented.

manifest.notes: This tests the array key contract, distinct from the element value contract. The runtime consequence remains real: an int key reaches strtoupper() under strict_types and throws. Psalm 6.20.0 and Mago 1.57.0 diagnose the call. The initial factory report counted PHPStan's level-9 silence as FN, but a later source and documentation audit corrected that classification without changing the fixture or its runtime result. PHPStan's configuration reference explicitly documents array-key as a benevolent union with deliberately lenient checking. In the pinned source, TypeNodeResolver.php:283-284 constructs that union; ArrayType.php:75-82 normalizes it to implicit mixed. The baseline checkImplicitMixed:false then deliberately accepts the key. An independent unchanged-source probe with checkImplicitMixed:true emits argument.type; an explicit int|string spelling also diagnoses. This is a documented dialect/configuration difference, not a missing implemented check, and is excluded consistently with the optional PHPDoc signature check. The older immutable factory reports retain the original FN for audit history; use the corrected cohort report for current claims. The Psalm candidate is a lead only: its suppressed upstream coercion is not the oracle for any tool.

the benevolent int|string key normalizes to implicit mixed; StrictMixedType becomes a checked plain union

transformCommonType / transformMixedType map a mixed type to StrictMixedType only when checkExplicitMixed (explicit mixed) or checkImplicitMixed (implicit mixed) is on; with both off the type is returned unchanged and an unspecified key stays lenient, which is why the level-9 run is silent here

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Runtime side of the ground truth. An array key is an int or a string and
// nothing else, so a caller whose array is typed array<array-key, int> may hand
// the callee an int key. The callee declares array<string, int> and uses every
// key as a string, so the call is the thing under test: the argument is legal
// PHP and the callee still fails on it.

require __DIR__ . '/../src/repro.php';

use function Bench\Arrays\ArrayKeyForStringKey\load;
use function Bench\Arrays\ArrayKeyForStringKey\render;

// The happy path: an all-string-keyed array renders.
if (render(['users' => 2]) !== 'USERS:2;') {
    fwrite(STDERR, "render(['users' => 2]) did not render 'USERS:2;'\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The argument's key set is a subset of array-key and really contains an int.
$counts = load();
$keys = array_keys($counts);

if (array_filter($keys, 'is_int') === []) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "the argument has no int key; the case is not exercised\n");
    exit(1);
}

foreach ($keys as $key) {
    if (!is_int($key) && !is_string($key)) {
        fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("unexpected key type %s\n", get_debug_type($key)));
        exit(1);
    }
}

// PHP does not check docblock key types either, so the call is accepted and the
// callee fails: strtoupper() receives the int key.
$type_error = null;
try {
    render([0 => 1]);
} catch (TypeError $error) {
    $type_error = $error;
}

if ($type_error === null) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "render() accepted an int key; the declared key type is not load-bearing\n");
    exit(1);
}

if (strpos($type_error->getMessage(), 'strtoupper') === false
    || strpos($type_error->getMessage(), 'string') === false) {
    fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("unexpected failure inside the callee: %s\n", $type_error->getMessage()));
    exit(1);
}

// Asymmetric control: a numeric string key does not survive as a string, so a
// callee cannot make its array<string> promise true by spelling the key as a
// string either.
$numeric = ['10' => 1];
if (array_keys($numeric) !== [10]) {
    fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("key normalisation changed: %s\n", var_export(array_keys($numeric), true)));
    exit(1);
}

printf(
    "array<array-key, int> argument keys include int 0; the array<string, int> callee fails: %s\n",
    $type_error->getMessage()
);
exit(0);

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Arrays\ArrayKeyForStringKey;

/** @param array<string, int> $counts */
function render(array $counts): string
{
    $out = '';
    foreach ($counts as $name => $count) {
        $out .= strtoupper($name) . ':' . $count . ';';
    }

    return $out;
}

/** @return array<array-key, int> */
function load(): array
{
    return [0 => 1, 'users' => 2];
}

function main(): string
{
    return render(load());
}

manifest.title: A canonical numeric string offset addresses the integer array key, so both key guards are reachable

ground_truth.statement: PHP casts an array key that is a canonical decimal integer string to int, so $data['10'] and $data[10] are one element. For [10 => 'kept'], array_key_exists('10', $data) and isset($data['10']) are both true and $data['10'] is 'kept'; neither guard is impossible and neither read is of type never. Non-canonical near misses ('10x', ' 10', '+10', '1.0') stay strings, so the claim is about canonical integers only.

manifest.notes: Mago 1.57.0 reports two diagnostics on code that demonstrably runs: impossible-condition on the array_key_exists('10', $data) guard and no-value on the guarded $data['10'] read, because its array-key reconciliation builds a string key where the shape carries the integer key 10. PHPStan 2.3.1 and Psalm 6.20.0 are silent. The runtime script is the neutral ground truth: it shows the string offset reaching the int key in both directions (read and write) and shows the non-canonical controls staying strings, so the guards are reachable and the reads are strings, not never. The pattern was taken from /home/abez/projects/mago-upstream-prep/repro/array-shape-numeric-string-key-normalization/repro.php; the comments in that reproducer were treated as a lead, not as evidence, and the fixture here is a clean-room rewrite that only keeps the pattern.

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Runtime side of the ground truth. PHP normalises an array key that is a
// canonical decimal integer string to int, so key '10' and key 10 address the
// same element and array_key_exists('10', ...) is true for an array with key
// 10. A docblock type is not enforced, so the fixture's guards decide: nothing
// throws and the guarded reads are the only reads.

require __DIR__ . '/../src/repro.php';

use function Bench\Arrays\NumericStringArrayKey\fetch;

$data = [10 => 'kept'];

if (array_keys($data) !== [10]) {
    fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("key normalisation changed: %s\n", var_export(array_keys($data), true)));
    exit(1);
}

if (!array_key_exists('10', $data)) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "array_key_exists('10', ...) is false although key 10 is set\n");
    exit(1);
}

if (!isset($data['10'])) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "isset(\$data['10']) is false although key 10 is set\n");
    exit(1);
}

if ($data['10'] !== 'kept') {
    fwrite(STDERR, "the string offset did not reach the int key\n");
    exit(1);
}

// A write through one spelling is visible through the other: one slot, not two.
$data['10'] = 'written';

if ($data[10] !== 'written') {
    fwrite(STDERR, "writing \$data['10'] did not update key 10\n");
    exit(1);
}

// Asymmetric control: only canonical decimal integer strings are cast. Typical
// near misses stay strings and are different keys from any int.
$other = ['10x' => 'a', ' 10' => 'b', '+10' => 'c', '1.0' => 'd'];

foreach (array_keys($other) as $key) {
    if (!is_string($key)) {
        fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("non-canonical key %s was cast to int\n", var_export($key, true)));
        exit(1);
    }
}

if (array_key_exists('10', $other)) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "a non-canonical '10'-like key was folded onto int 10\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The fixture itself runs: neither guard throws, and both accepted reads are
// 'kept' -> the two call sites the case is about are exercised.
fetch([10 => 'kept']);

printf("key 10 is reachable as '10' (array_key_exists, isset, read, write); %d near miss(es) stayed strings\n", count($other));
exit(0);

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Arrays\NumericStringArrayKey;

function accept_string(string $_): void {}

/** @param array{10?: string} $data */
function fetch(array $data): void
{
    if (array_key_exists('10', $data)) {
        accept_string($data[10]);
    }

    if (isset($data['10'])) {
        accept_string($data['10']);
    }
}

manifest.title: An array<int, scalar> argument cannot satisfy a parameter declared array<string>

ground_truth.statement: PHP does not enforce a docblock element type, so an array that the caller declares array<int, scalar> may hold a float. The callee declares array<string> and passes every element to strlen(), and under strict_types that call fails with a TypeError on the float. Passing an argument of type array<int, scalar> into a parameter of type array<string> is therefore unsound: the parameter's declared element type is a contract the argument cannot meet, and a diagnostic belongs on the call.

manifest.notes: The rule under test is the value dimension of an array argument's type: a parameter declared array<string> promises its elements are strings, and an argument declared array<int, scalar> may hold a float or a bool instead. manifest.title: Strict in_array() over a literal haystack narrows the needle to the string elements

ground_truth.statement: in_array($x, $y, true) compares with ===. In this fixture the haystack elements are 'a', 'b' or an int, so a true result means the needle is identical to one of them, and neither a bool nor a numeric string can be: for string|bool $x inside the guard, $x is 'a' or 'b'. Passing it to a parameter typed "a"|"b" is therefore sound, and no diagnostic belongs on that call.

manifest.notes: Mago 1.57.0 reports possibly-invalid-argument on the guarded call and describes the argument as numeric-string|'a'|'b', i.e. it reconciles the needle against a numeric-string alternative of the haystack even though the comparison is strict. PHPStan 2.3.1 and Psalm 6.20.0 narrow to 'a'|'b' and stay silent. The runtime script carries the asymmetric control the claim needs: the same needle/haystack pair under the default loose comparison matches ('1' is in [1]) while the strict form does not, so the third argument - not the values alone - is what makes the narrowing hold. <?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Runtime side of the ground truth. With the third argument true, in_array()
// compares with ===, so a value is in the haystack only if it is identical to
// an element. The fixture's needle is declared string|bool and its haystack
// elements are 'a', 'b' or an int; over exactly those needle types a true result
// means the needle is 'a' or 'b', because no bool and no string is identical to
// an int.

require __DIR__ . '/../src/repro.php';

use function Bench\Arrays\StrictInArrayNarrowing\narrow;

$haystacks = [
    ['a', 'b', 1],
    ['a', 'b'],
    [1, 0],
    [],
    ['b', 2, 'a'],
];

// The needle sample mirrors the declared type of the fixture's parameter.
$needles = [true, false, 'a', 'b', '1', '0', '', 'a1', 'b0'];

$matches = 0;
foreach ($haystacks as $haystack) {
    foreach ($needles as $needle) {
        if (!in_array($needle, $haystack, true)) {
            continue;
        }

        $matches++;
        if ($needle !== 'a' && $needle !== 'b') {
            fwrite(STDERR, sprintf(
                "strict in_array matched %s in %s; the narrowing claim is false\n",
                var_export($needle, true),
                var_export($haystack, true)
            ));
            exit(1);
        }
    }
}

if ($matches === 0) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "the sample produced no match at all; the claim is not exercised\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The third argument is what carries the claim, not the values alone. An int
// needle does match an int element under ===, and the same '1'/1 pair matches
// only in the loose form.
if (!in_array(1, [1], true)) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "strict in_array(1, [1]) is false\n");
    exit(1);
}

if (in_array('1', [1], true)) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "strict in_array('1', [1]) is true; strings and ints are not compared with ===\n");
    exit(1);
}

if (!in_array('1', [1], false)) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "loose in_array('1', [1]) is false; the loose control is wrong\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The fixture's guard is exercised for a match and for a miss.
narrow('a', ['a', 'b', 1]);
narrow(false, ['a', 'b', 1]);

printf("%d strict match(es) over %d needle/haystack pair(s), all 'a'/'b'\n", $matches, count($haystacks) * count($needles));
exit(0);

/** @param "a"|"b" $_ */
function accept_ab(string $_): void {}

/**
 * @param string|bool $x

manifest.title: A callable is not assignable to Closure, although a Closure is a callable

ground_truth.statement: PHP's callable pseudo-type covers closures, strings and arrays, while \Closure is one class. A value that is only known to be callable is therefore not assignable to a \Closure parameter: 'phpversion' is callable but is not an instance of Closure, and both from_string_literal() and from_callable('strlen') throw a TypeError when they reach keep(). The asymmetric control is a real closure, which is accepted and returns.

manifest.notes: A green row kept as a regression guard: all three analyzers separate callable from Closure and report both the literal string (line 19, a definite violation) and the callable-typed parameter (line 14, where the value may be a string), while line 24 - an actual closure - stays silent for all three. The runtime script also shows that 'phpversion' really is usable as a callable (is_callable and call_user_func), so the case is about the class boundary, not about callability. Psalm calls the line-14 report ArgumentTypeCoercion rather than InvalidArgument, which is its own code for a coerced argument; that is a naming difference, not a disagreement about the fact.

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Runtime side of the ground truth. A string function name is a callable but
// not a Closure: the callable pseudo-type is a union of closures, strings and
// arrays, so a value typed callable is not accepted where \Closure is required.

require __DIR__ . '/../src/repro.php';

use function Bench\Assignability\CallableNotClosure\from_callable;
use function Bench\Assignability\CallableNotClosure\from_closure;
use function Bench\Assignability\CallableNotClosure\from_string_literal;
use function Bench\Assignability\CallableNotClosure\keep;

// The string is callable - the fixture is not about "not callable" - but it is
// not an instance of Closure.
if (!is_callable('phpversion')) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "'phpversion' is not callable; the control is wrong\n");
    exit(1);
}

if (call_user_func('phpversion') === '') {
    fwrite(STDERR, "calling 'phpversion' produced no version string\n");
    exit(1);
}

if ('phpversion' instanceof Closure) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "a string function name is an instance of Closure\n");
    exit(1);
}

// A definite violation: the literal reaches the \Closure parameter.
try {
    from_string_literal();
    fwrite(STDERR, "keep('phpversion') did not throw\n");
    exit(1);
} catch (TypeError $error) {
    // expected: the string is not a Closure
}

// A possible violation: a value typed only as callable may be a string.
try {
    from_callable('strlen');
    fwrite(STDERR, "keep(callable) with a string callable did not throw\n");
    exit(1);
} catch (TypeError $error) {
    // expected: the value is a string, which is not a Closure
}

// Asymmetric control: a real closure is accepted and returned.
$closure = from_closure();

if (!$closure instanceof Closure || $closure() !== 'ok') {
    fwrite(STDERR, "a closure was not accepted for the \\Closure parameter\n");
    exit(1);
}

if (keep(static fn (): string => 'ok')() !== 'ok') {
    fwrite(STDERR, "the closure control did not survive the parameter\n");
    exit(1);
}

printf("'phpversion' is callable but not a Closure; the closure control was accepted\n");
exit(0);

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Assignability\CallableNotClosure;

function keep(\Closure $fn): \Closure
{
    return $fn;
}

function from_callable(callable $fn): \Closure
{
    return keep($fn);
}

function from_string_literal(): \Closure
{
    return keep('phpversion');
}

function from_closure(): \Closure

    return keep(static fn (): string => 'ok');
}

manifest.title: An overriding method must not widen the return type its parent documents

ground_truth.statement: Shelter::adopt() documents @return Dog and BadShelter::adopt() documents @return Animal, returning a Cat. PHP enforces only the native signature (Animal -> Animal is legal), so the widening is silent until a caller that believes the parent's contract calls a Dog-only method: wake(new BadShelter()) throws Error because Cat has no bark(). The override is therefore not assignable to the parent contract it claims to implement.

phpstan.reason: In this baseline configuration PHPStan deliberately suppresses maybe-compatible PHPDoc override checks: reportMaybesInMethodSignatures defaults to false. MethodSignatureRule emits method.childReturnType for this widening only with that optional flag enabled. This is an excluded configuration-scope difference, not evidence that PHPStan lacks the rule.

manifest.notes: Psalm 6.20.0 (LessSpecificImplementedReturnType) and Mago 1.57.0 (incompatible-return-type) report the widened override. PHPStan 2.3.1 is silent at the baseline level-9 configuration because reportMaybesInMethodSignatures is false (conf/config.neon:100). Its MethodSignatureRule explicitly gates maybe-compatible overrides on that option. Enabling the option yields method.childReturnType; therefore its baseline silence is a documented configuration-scope divergence, excluded from the defect denominator. The fixture and runtime consequence remain unchanged: wake(new BadShelter()) throws when the widened override breaks the parent's PHPDoc contract. The benchmark records both the concrete program defect and which configured checks promise to diagnose it.

sources.note: Psalm documents the rule with an interface-implementation example

OverridingMethodRule.php line 376 gates the PHPDoc signature rule; MethodSignatureRule.php reports a maybe compatibility only when reportMaybesInMethodSignatures is true, and conf/config.neon line 100 sets it false (conf/config.level3.neon line 9 turns checkPhpDocMethodSignatures on)

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Runtime side of the ground truth. Shelter documents adopt() as returning
// Dog; BadShelter overrides it and documents Animal, returning a Cat. PHP
// enforces only the native signature (Animal -> Animal is legal), so the
// widening is silent until a caller that believes the parent's contract calls a
// Dog-only method.

require __DIR__ . '/../src/repro.php';

use Bench\Assignability\DocblockReturnCovariance\BadShelter;
use Bench\Assignability\DocblockReturnCovariance\Cat;
use Bench\Assignability\DocblockReturnCovariance\Dog;
use Bench\Assignability\DocblockReturnCovariance\Shelter;
use function Bench\Assignability\DocblockReturnCovariance\wake;

if (!(new Shelter())->adopt() instanceof Dog) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "Shelter::adopt() does not return a Dog; the parent promise is wrong\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The parent contract holds, so wake() works against the parent.
if (wake(new Shelter()) !== 'woof') {
    fwrite(STDERR, "wake(new Shelter()) did not return 'woof'\n");
    exit(1);
}

$widened = (new BadShelter())->adopt();

if (!$widened instanceof Cat) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "BadShelter::adopt() did not return a Cat\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The consequence the case is about: a caller that trusts the parent's
// documented return type crashes on the widened override.
try {
    wake(new BadShelter());
} catch (Error $error) {
    if (strpos($error->getMessage(), 'bark') === false) {
        fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("unexpected Error: %s\n", $error->getMessage()));
        exit(1);
    }

    printf("BadShelter::adopt() returns a Cat, so wake() throws: %s\n", $error->getMessage());
    exit(0);
}

fwrite(STDERR, "wake(new BadShelter()) returned; the widened override did not break the caller\n");
exit(1);
files.src/repro.php:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Assignability\DocblockReturnCovariance;

class Animal {}

class Dog extends Animal
{
    public function bark(): string
    {
        return 'woof';
    }
}

class Cat extends Animal {}

class Shelter
{
    /** @return Dog */
    public function adopt(): Animal
    {
        return new Dog();
    }
}

class BadShelter extends Shelter
{
    /** @return Animal */
    #[\Override]
    public function adopt(): Animal
    {
        return new Cat();
    }
}

function wake(Shelter $shelter): string
{
    $animal = $shelter->adopt();

    return $animal->bark();
}

ground_truth.statement: A Closure and an invokable Handler are objects and enter the true branch; the callable string strlen is not an object and enters the false branch. Both outcomes are reachable, and the is_object guard makes the object parameter call sound.

manifest.notes: The runtime exercises both object forms and a non-object callable. No tool-specific extension is needed.

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Runtime side of the ground truth: the branch is reachable, which is decided
// by calling it with the two object shapes a callable can have. The control
// shows that a plain callable-string does take the other path, so the true
// result is not a tautology of the fixture.

require __DIR__ . '/../src/repro.php';

use Bench\Callables\IsObjectOnCallableParameter\Handler;

use function Bench\Callables\IsObjectOnCallableParameter\quacks;

$closure = static function (): string {
    return 'closed';
};

$cases = [
    [$closure, true, 'Closure'],
    [new Handler(), true, 'Handler'],
    ['strlen', false, 'callable-string'],
];

foreach ($cases as [$value, $expected, $label]) {
    $actual = quacks($value);
    if ($actual !== $expected) {
        fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("quacks(%s) = %s, expected %s\n", $label,
            var_export($actual, true), var_export($expected, true)));
        exit(1);
    }
    if (!is_callable($value)) {
        fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("%s is not callable, the fixture could not be driven\n", $label));
        exit(1);
    }
}

printf("is_object() branch reached for %d of %d callable shape(s)\n", 2, count($cases));
exit(0);
files.src/repro.php:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Callables\IsObjectOnCallableParameter;

function accept_object(object $_): void {}

final class Handler
{
    public function __invoke(): string
    {
        return 'handled';
    }
}

/**
 * A callable is a Closure, an object with __invoke, a function name or a
 * method array. The first two are objects, so is_object() has a reachable true
 * outcome for a declared callable parameter and the branch is not dead.
 */
function quacks(callable $fn): bool
{
    if (is_object($fn)) {
        accept_object($fn);

        return true;
    }

    return false;
}

files.src/repro.php:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Callables\NegatedIsCallableRemovesFunctionName;

/** @param list<int> $_ */
function accept_array(array $_): void {}

/**
 * The value is either the function name 'strlen' or the array [1]. is_callable()
 * is true for the function name and false for [1], which is not a valid
 * callback array, so the code after the guard only ever sees [1] and
 * accept_array() is satisfied.
 */
function quacks(bool $useFunctionName): void
{
    $value = $useFunctionName ? 'strlen' : [1];

    if (is_callable($value)) {
        return;
    }

    accept_array($value);
}

manifest.title: PHPStan reads a finally assignment as if it never ran

ground_truth.statement: A `finally` block runs while an exception unwinds towards an outer `catch`, so $cleaned is true when the ternary reads it: the condition is always true and cleaned_flag() always returns 1.

allowed.reason: The finally assignment makes the condition true. A warning that it is always true is correct; a warning that it is always false must still count as a false positive.

files.src/repro.php:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\DeadCode\FinallyAssignment;

/**
 * The inner `finally` block runs while the exception unwinds, before the outer
 * `catch` gets control, so $cleaned is true when the last statement reads it.
 * The ternary condition is therefore always true.
 */
function cleaned_flag(): int
{
    $cleaned = false;

    try {
        try {
            throw new \RuntimeException('a');
        } finally {
            $cleaned = true;
        }
    } catch (\Throwable) {
    }

    return $cleaned ? 1 : 0;
}

manifest.title: BackedEnum::tryFrom() is nullable, but not for a known backing literal

ground_truth.statement: BackedEnum::tryFrom() returns the case when the backing value is known and null otherwise. The fixture passes the literal 'active', which is Status::Active's backing value, so the result of that call is never null and passing it to the Status parameter is sound; passing the result of tryFrom($raw) for an arbitrary string is not, because that value can be null. The runtime script decides both directions: tryFrom('active') is Status::Active, tryFrom('nope') is null and label(null) throws a TypeError, while from('nope') throws ValueError instead of returning null.

manifest.notes: PHPStan 2.3.1 models tryFrom() conditionally on a literal argument and reports only the genuinely nullable call (line 25) - a correct row. Psalm 6.20.0 and Mago 1.57.0 report PossiblyNullArgument / possibly-null-argument on line 20 as well, where the runtime proof shows the value is Status::Active and can never be null; that report is the recorded false positive, and the forbidden predicate keeps the case honest instead of quietly widening the expectation. The line-20 claim is not a missing optional warning: the value is not merely usually non-null, it is decidable from the literal and the enum's backing values. PHPStan's own fixture tests/PHPStan/Analyser/nsrt/enums.php models the call with a variable subject as 'X|null', which is why the switch to a literal matters here.

declare(strict_types=1);
abstract class Entity {}
final class Product extends Entity {}

abstract class Mapper {
    /** @param T $entity */

manifest.title: A class-level template type argument substitutes into the member's return type

ground_truth.statement: Box declares @template T with @return T on get(), so the annotation @param Box<Cat> tells the caller that get() hands back a Cat, and the member access that follows has to be resolved against Cat - which has no bark(). The runtime script decides both halves independently of any analyzer: a value taken from a Box<Dog> dispatches Dog::bark() and returns 'woof', a value taken from a Box<Cat> dispatches Cat::meow() and returns 'meow' (so the substituted type is the class the annotation names, not mixed), and the same get()->bark() access on the Box<Cat> side fails with 'Error: Call to undefined method Cat::bark()'. Callers cannot weaken this: the class-level template is part of the annotation the callee published, exactly like a native parameter type.

manifest.notes: The rule under test is template substitution into a member's type at a use site: the same member access, on the same generic class, with only the type argument changed. All three tools substitute and report, under their own code: PHPStan 2.3.1 method.notFound, Psalm 6.20.0 UndefinedMethod, Mago 1.57.0 non-existent-method. The two forbidden predicates are the asymmetric controls and they are what makes the row about substitution rather than about member access: line 41 is the identical get()->bark() on Box<Dog>, which must stay silent, and line 53 is get()->meow() on Box<Cat>, which must stay silent too. The second control is the harder one - a tool that treated the declared @return mixed of get() as the receiver would report meow() as undefined on mixed and fail the case - so a tool cannot pass by guessing. The required predicates also pin the substituted class in the message ('Cat::bark' / 'bark ... Cat'), so an undefined-method report that does not name Cat does not satisfy the case. Every diagnostic the three tools produced is claimed by a predicate; nothing is acknowledged away and nothing is widened. No existing case in this corpus uses an undefined-method rule class, and none of the other generics cases covers member resolution on a substituted type argument (they cover inference from an argument and a declared bound). The round's source material, Mago's analyzer test suite, is a directory of fixtures without catalogue candidate IDs, and no catalogue lead covers this rule, so no source_candidate_id is recorded.

manifest.title: A covariant template used in a parameter position makes the declared variance unsound

ground_truth.statement: Bag declares @template-covariant T, which promises that a Bag<Dog> may be used wherever a Bag<Animal> is expected, and it also declares push() with @param T, a write position. Those two promises cannot both hold. The runtime script executes the program the declarations license: put_cat() is typed Bag<Animal>, the covariant promise makes the caller's Bag<Dog> acceptable to it, put_cat() stores a Cat in that box, and the caller - whose annotation says Bag<Dog> - reads a Cat back. A Cat is not a Dog (the script checks the sibling relationship directly), and adopt() declares the native return type Dog, so the call fails with 'adopt(): Return value must be of type Dog, Cat returned'. A fresh Bag constructed with a Dog does read back a Dog, so the failure is caused by the declared write position and not by the widening on its own.

manifest.notes: The rule under test is the consistency of a declared generic variance: @template-covariant T means 'every reader of a Bag<Dog> may treat it as a Bag<Animal>', and that is sound only while T never appears in a write position. PHP has no generics, so the declaration itself cannot fail; what fails is the program the declaration grants, and the case's neutral ground truth for all three tools is that program. The three tools report it under different codes and on adjacent lines of the same declaration - PHPStan 2.3.1 generics.variance on the push() signature (line 30), Psalm 6.20.0 InvalidTemplateParam on the @param T docblock line (29), Mago 1.57.0 invalid-template-parameter on the signature (30) - so the row is green with a code and site split rather than a defect. The forbidden predicate on line 51 is the asymmetric control: that call is the covariance widening itself, which the declaration licenses, and a tool that reports it as an argument mismatch instead of reporting the declaration would be pointing at the site the annotation permits. Building a Bag<Dog> that goes through the covariant view into put_cat() is exercised by the runtime script, so no predicate is acknowledged away and nothing is widened. Distinct from the two existing generics cases: generics/template-inference-from-argument tests an inferred function template reaching a native consumer, generics/template-bound-violation tests a value against a declared bound, and neither touches a variance declaration. The round's source material is Mago's analyzer test suite, a directory of fixtures without catalogue candidate IDs, so no source_candidate_id is recorded; the closest catalogue leads cover bound enforcement and @extends arity, which are different rules, and are not claimed here.

sources.note: pattern source for a sound @template-covariant declaration (T is only read there, and Mago expects no diagnostic); this fixture keeps the declaration and adds the write position that makes it unsound. Rewritten, not copied, and Mago's suite carries no expectation for the write-position rule (grep for invalid-template-parameter in that directory returns only @extends/@implements arity fixtures), so Mago is judged here by the runtime proof like the other two.

shows that Mago's suite treats variance declarations as part of the supported dialect (the mirror-image contrapositive annotation), which is why this fixture does not use mode 'unsupported' for any tool

declare(strict_types=1);

// Runtime side of the ground truth. Bag declares @template-covariant T, so the
// declaration promises that a Bag<Dog> may be used wherever a Bag<Animal> is
// expected - that is what covariance buys the caller. It also declares push()
// with @param T, a write position. Those two promises cannot both hold: put_cat()
// accepts a Bag<Animal> and writes a Cat through that view, the original holder
// of a Bag<Dog> then reads a Cat where its annotation promises a Dog, and the
// native return type of adopt() enforces exactly that promise.

require __DIR__ . '/../src/repro.php';

use function Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\adopt;
use function Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\put_cat;
use function Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\run;

use Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\Bag;
use Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\Cat;
use Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition\Dog;

// The sibling classes are unrelated: a Cat is not a Dog, so a Cat written into a
// Bag<Dog> makes the caller's guarantee false independently of any analyzer.
if ((new Cat()) instanceof Dog) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "Cat is a Dog; the fixture no longer witnesses the write\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The honest path: a fresh Bag<Dog> holding a Dog reads back a Dog.
$fresh = new Bag(new Dog());
if (!$fresh->get() instanceof Dog) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "a fresh Bag constructed with a Dog did not read back a Dog\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The write through the widened view: put_cat() is typed Bag<Animal>, which
// covariance makes the Bag<Dog> acceptable to, and it stores a Cat in the very
// box the caller annotated as Bag<Dog>.
$holder = new Bag(new Dog());
put_cat($holder);
if (!$holder->get() instanceof Cat) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "put_cat() did not write a Cat through the widened view\n");
    exit(1);
}

// The consequence: adopt() is annotated Bag<Dog> and declares a native Dog
// return type, so the Cat that covariance let in reaches that return type and
// the call fails. This is the fact the case is about - the covariant
// declaration plus a write position is unsound, not merely unidiomatic.
$type_error = null;
try {
    run();
} catch (TypeError $error) {
    $type_error = $error;
}

if ($type_error === null) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "run() returned; the Cat did not reach adopt()'s Dog return type\n");
    exit(1);
}

if (strpos($type_error->getMessage(), 'adopt') === false
    || strpos($type_error->getMessage(), 'Dog') === false
    || strpos($type_error->getMessage(), 'Cat') === false) {
    fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("unexpected failure: %s\n", $type_error->getMessage()));
    exit(1);
}

printf(
    "put_cat() stored a Cat in a Bag<Dog> through the covariant widening; adopt() failed on its Dog return type: %s\n",
    $type_error->getMessage()
);
exit(0);

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Generics\CovariantTemplateInWritePosition;

class Animal
{
}

final class Dog extends Animal
{
}

final class Cat extends Animal
{
}

/**
 * @template-covariant T
 */
final class Bag
{
    /** @param T $value */
    public function __construct(private mixed $value)
    {
    }

    /** @param T $value */
    public function push(mixed $value): void
    {
        $this->value = $value;
    }

    /** @return T */
    public function get(): mixed
    {
        return $this->value;
    }
}

/** @param Bag<Animal> $bag */
function put_cat(Bag $bag): void
{
    $bag->push(new Cat());
}

/** @param Bag<Dog> $dogs */
function adopt(Bag $dogs): Dog
{
    put_cat($dogs);

    return $dogs->get();
}

function run(): Dog
{
    return adopt(new Bag(new Dog()));
}

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\LegacyPatterns\ArrayFilterStringCallableLosesList;

/**
 * @param list<int> $_
 */
function accept_list_of_ints(array $_): void {}

/**
 * Legacy code filters with a string callable and then treats the result as a
 * list. array_filter() keeps the original keys, so removing an earlier element
 * while retaining a later one leaves a hole and the result is not a list.
 *
 * @param list<mixed> $rows
 */
function only_ints(array $rows): void
{
    $filtered = array_filter($rows, 'is_int');
    accept_list_of_ints($filtered);
}

manifest.title: count() on a parameter that is only iterable throws for a non-Countable Traversable

ground_truth.statement: count() accepts an array or a Countable. An `iterable` parameter may be a Generator or another Traversable that does not implement Countable, and count() throws a TypeError for it; the fixture therefore cannot count its parameter unconditionally.

manifest.notes: PHPStan 2.3.1 (argument.type) and Mago 1.57.0 (possibly-invalid-argument) reject the call; Psalm 6.20.0 reports nothing for an `iterable` parameter, although its own callmap gives count() the parameter type `Countable|array<array-key, mixed>`, it reports InvalidArgument for a `Traversable` or `Generator` parameter, and it reports PossiblyInvalidArgument for a `Countable|Traversable` parameter - which is why the expected code here is PossiblyInvalidArgument and not InvalidArgument. The silence is therefore a false negative against Psalm's own documented signature, not a by-design divergence. runtime/check.php is the neutral ground truth: it calls the fixture with a Generator and the call throws a TypeError.

namespace Bench\LegacyPatterns\LooseComparisonWithZero;

function accept_string(string $_): void {}

namespace Bench\Narrowing\IsNumericAfterIsInt;

/**
 * The right operand of && can never change the result once the left operand
 * has been evaluated: is_int($c) narrows $c to int, and is_numeric() is true

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Narrowing\NegatedInstanceofUnrelatedClass;

class Alpha {}

class Beta {}

/**
 * Alpha and Beta are unrelated: neither extends the other, and PHP gives every
 * object exactly one inheritance chain. No instance of Alpha - nor of any
 * subclass of Alpha - is an instance of Beta, so the negation is always true.

function is_not_beta(Alpha $value): bool

manifest.title: a variable tested only in an elseif branch stays nullable after the structure

ground_truth.statement: The elseif condition is only evaluated when the first condition was false. With $a non-null and $b null the first branch runs, $b is never tested and execution continues with $b still null, so the final `$b === null` is true on a reachable path.

manifest.notes: A tool that assumes the post-structure state satisfies every branch condition removes null from $b and then calls the final check redundant and its body dead. The first runtime case decides the opposite. This is the same class of unsound branch merging as the open upstream report for Mago (COORDINATION.json R56 / repro/elseif-else-return-unsound-variable-narrowing), but the expectation here rests on the runtime proof only.

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Runtime side of the ground truth. The first sample is the decisive one: it
// reaches the final check with $b === null, so the check is neither redundant
// nor unreachable. The others show that the other reachable states still
// behave, which keeps the fixture from passing for the wrong reason.

use function Bench\Nullability\ElseifElseReturnKeepsPossibleNull\is_null_after;

$cases = [
    ['value', null, true],   // first branch taken, $b never tested, still null
    [null, 'value', false],  // second branch taken, $b is non-null
    [null, null, false],     // else branch returns before the check
    ['a', 'b', false],       // first branch taken, $b is non-null
];

foreach ($cases as [$a, $b, $expected]) {
    $actual = is_null_after($a, $b);
    if ($actual !== $expected) {
        fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("is_null_after(%s, %s) = %s, expected %s\n",
            var_export($a, true), var_export($b, true), var_export($actual, true),
            var_export($expected, true)));
        exit(1);
    }

printf("is_null_after() reached the final check with null in %d case(s)\n", count($cases));
exit(0);
files.src/repro.php:
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Nullability\ElseifElseReturnKeepsPossibleNull;

/**
 * Execution continues past the structure when at least one of the two
 * conditions held - not when both did. With $a !== null and $b === null the
 * first branch runs, $b was never tested, and the final check still has a true
 * outcome.
 */
function is_null_after(?string $a, ?string $b): bool
{
    if ($a !== null) {
        $a = trim($a);
    } elseif ($b !== null) {
        $b = trim($b);
    } else {
        return false;
    }

    return $b === null;
}

manifest.title: '' == null is true but '' === null is false, so the strict check inside the loose guard is not redundant

ground_truth.statement: In PHP 8, comparing null with a non-empty string is false and comparing it with '' is true, while '' === null is false. Inside the `$value == null` branch the value can therefore be '', so the inner `$value === null` has a reachable false outcome and the code behind it runs.

allowed.reason: Mago reports these two codes for any loose comparison whose operand may be null, and its own test suite expects them: crates/analyzer/tests/cases/flow_loose_eq_null.php expects `possibly-null-operand` and `null-operand` for `if ($v == null)` on a `null|int` parameter, and issue_1757.php expects `possibly-null-operand` for `$i == 0` on `?int`. Intended output, not a claim about this fixture. The redundant-condition reports on line 15 are a different matter and stay counted.

manifest.notes: The loose-null guard is a legacy defensive pattern. A tool that treats `== null` like `=== null` reports the inner check as redundant and the branch as dead; the runtime script shows both are alive. The '0' sample is a deliberate control: '0' == null is false and must not enter the outer branch. This string/null rule is not a PHP 8 change. The finding is independently corroborated by upstream report PR 2579 (https://github.com/carthage-software/mago/pull/2579), which describes the same root cause; the runtime proof here was derived from the fixture first.

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Nullability\LooseNullGuardKeepsEmptyString;

/**
 * The loose comparison is true for null and for the empty string, so inside the
 * branch the strict `=== null` check still has a reachable false outcome: it is
 * not redundant, and the code after it runs for ''.

function classify(?string $value): string
{
    if ($value == null) {
        if ($value === null) {
            return 'null';
        }

        return 'loose-null';
    }

    return 'string';
}

manifest.title: a > comparison against 0 removes null from a nullable int

ground_truth.statement: When comparing null with an integer, PHP converts both operands to bool. Thus null > 0 compares false > false and is false. The input domain is {null} plus {int}, so null never enters the branch and the argument passed there is an int. The runtime control null > -1 is also false, distinguishing this rule from numeric conversion of null to zero.

allowed.reason: Mago warns on every comparison whose operand may be null, whatever the comparison is used for. That is its intended output: crates/analyzer/tests/cases/issue_2434.php in the Mago repository expects exactly `possibly-null-operand` for `if ($x > 0)` with a `?int $x` parameter, which is this line. The warning does not claim the branch can receive null, and Mago correctly reports nothing for the accept_int() call, which is what this case tests.

manifest.notes: From the field: `if ($a > 0)` on a nullable int is a common legacy null guard. The null case is a single value, so the runtime check decides it rather than sampling it. Mago's null-operand warning is acknowledged above with the upstream test that documents it as intended (basis: upstream_test).

// is false, no null can reach the branch. For an int the comparison is an

    fwrite(STDERR, "null/int comparison was numeric instead of boolean\n");
    exit(1);
}

foreach ([null, 0, -1, PHP_INT_MIN] as $sample) {
    if (quacks($sample) !== false) {
        fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("quacks(%s) entered the branch\n", var_export($sample, true)));
        exit(1);
    }
}

foreach ([1, 2, PHP_INT_MAX] as $sample) {
    if (quacks($sample) !== true) {
        fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("quacks(%s) did not enter the branch\n", var_export($sample, true)));
        exit(1);
    }
}

echo "null > 0 is false; quacks() entered the branch for positive ints only\n";
exit(0);

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace Bench\Nullability\RelationalComparisonExcludesNull;

function accept_int(int $_): void {}

/**
 * When null is compared with an integer, both operands convert to bool.
 * false > false is false, so null never enters the branch: inside it the
 * parameter is an int and accept_int() is satisfied.
 */
function quacks(?int $value): bool
{

        accept_int($value);

    return false;
}

manifest.title: fn-malformed-phpdoc (clean-room semantics)

ground_truth.statement: Under the PHP-FIG proposed PHPDoc grammar, type-expression = type *("|" type) *("&" type), so a trailing union separator without another type is malformed. PHP itself ignores the comment; the valid array<int, Group> annotation is the control.

allowed.reason: Ignoring the malformed annotation leaves a bare native array parameter without an element type. This is a correct secondary completeness diagnostic.

manifest.notes: The local source is a lead, not an oracle. The neutral grammar is proposed PSR-5 Appendix A, not a ratified PHP standard. It requires a type after every union separator. phpDocumentor's permissive ABNF admits a trailing separator and cannot establish this stricter criterion. Runtime proves only that PHP ignores the comment. Measured with PHP 8.3.35, PHPStan 2.3.1, Psalm 6.20.0 and Mago 1.57.0. PHPStan and Psalm diagnose the malformed annotation; Mago omits invalid-docblock. Missing syntax diagnostics are measured as broad behavior gaps, not a claim that Mago promises rejection of every malformed function annotation. The source has three malformed forms; this minimal fixture isolates the dangling union form.
